record.paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
record.original_question: Which low-energy neutrino-beam facility strategy can provide the intense beams needed to address open neutrino-nucleus interaction questions: a conventional source based on pion and muon decay, or a beta-beam source based on accelerated beta-decaying nuclei that produces pure electron-neutrino or electron-antineutrino beams with tunable mean energy Eν ≃ 2γQβ?

evidence.quote: In order to address these (and other) open questions, one needs a facility producing intense low-energy neutrinos.
There are essentially two options for a facility producing low-energy neutrino beams: either a conventional one, based on the decay of pions and muons, or beta-beams [28].
Conventional sources provide us with neutrinos of different flavours, while beta-beams produce pure electron neutrino (or anti-neutrino) beams.
Beta-beams have the specific feature that the neutrino mean energy depends on the ion acceleration according to Eν ≃ 2γQβ, where γ is the Lorentz gamma factor and Qβ is the beta-decay Q-value.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the design problem of providing intense low-energy neutrino beams (with neutrino energies on the order of tens of MeV) suitable for systematic studies of neutrino–nucleus interactions. Two candidate facility strategies are available:

(A) A conventional stopped-pion/decay-at-rest source, in which an intense proton beam impinges on a target producing pions that decay (π⁺ → μ⁺ν_μ followed by μ⁺ → e⁺ν_e \bar ν_μ), yielding a mixed flux of ν_μ, ν_e and \bar ν_μ with a known Michel-like spectrum capped near m_μ/2 ≈ 52.8 MeV.

(B) A beta-beam source, in which radioactive β-decaying ions (e.g. ⁶He for \bar ν_e, ¹⁸Ne for ν_e) are accelerated to a Lorentz factor γ and allowed to decay in a storage ring, producing a pure, collimated ν_e or \bar ν_e beam whose mean energy in the laboratory frame is E_ν ≃ 2γ Q_β, where Q_β is the β-decay endpoint energy of the parent ion.

Determine which of the two strategies — the conventional pion/muon-decay source (A) or the beta-beam source (B) — is the appropriate choice for delivering the intense, well-characterized low-energy neutrino fluxes required to resolve the outstanding open questions in neutrino–nucleus interaction physics, taking into account flavor content, spectral purity, tunability of the mean energy through the Lorentz factor γ, achievable intensity, and systematic control.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a strategic/comparative one about future experimental facilities rather than a theorem to be proved. Both conventional stopped-pion sources (e.g. SNS/COHERENT, ESSnuSB low-energy program) and beta-beam concepts have been studied extensively, and they are generally regarded as complementary rather than mutually exclusive. No single, definitive community-wide selection of one strategy over the other has been made; beta-beams remain a proposal, while conventional decay-at-rest sources are operational. The status of the underlying decision is therefore best characterized as unknown/unsettled.
